key_facts: **Telogen effluvium** is diffuse shedding about **2–3 months after a trigger**, when many follicles shift into telogen together.
Triggers: childbirth, febrile illness (including COVID-19), surgery, crash diets, iron deficiency, thyroid disease, new drugs.
Positive **hair-pull test** (more than 4–6 club hairs) in the acute phase; no scarring, no miniaturisation.
Check ferritin, thyroid function and full blood count if the trigger is unclear.
Reassure: regrowth over **6–12 months** once the trigger has gone; chronic TE lasts longer than 6 months.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Telogen effluvium (TE)** is non-scarring **diffuse** shedding of telogen (club) hairs. Acute TE follows a trigger by about **2–3 months**. Chronic TE lasts beyond 6 months.

**Androgenetic (pattern) hair loss** is the other common diffuse-looking thinning of mid-life — full UK IP detail and Module 6 Week 6 photos live on [androgenetic alopecia](condition:androgenetic-alopecia). This page only sketches the DDx so Week 3 teaching stays joined up without duplicating that photo set.

sub: Common at any age, more often reported by women.
Postpartum shedding affects many women 2–4 months after delivery.

ul: Classic triggers: high fever, COVID/flu-like illness, major surgery, postpartum (including when stopping breastfeeding), crash diets, haemorrhage, new drugs (retinoids, anticoagulants, antithyroid, beta-blockers, some anticonvulsants — check BNF), severe stress.
Iron deficiency, thyroid disease and other metabolic insults.
Chronic TE: ongoing trigger or idiopathic; overlap with female pattern loss is common.
Physiological stress, hormonal change, nutritional deficiency or drugs (retinoids, anticoagulants, beta-blockers, stopping the combined pill).
**"Shedding means I'll go bald"**: follicles are alive and will regrow.
**"Hair supplements cure it"**: only replace a proven deficiency.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A shock **synchronises** hair cycles so many hairs rest and then fall together.

mech.t: Normally about 85–90% of scalp hairs are growing (anagen) and 10–15% resting (telogen) at any time.
A physiological shock pushes many anagen follicles into early **telogen** at once.
Telogen lasts about 3 months, so club hairs shed in large numbers 2–3 months after the trigger.
New anagen hairs push out the old ones; short regrowing hairs at the hairline are a good sign.

histo: Biopsy only if unclear: normal follicle numbers with an increased proportion of telogen follicles; no miniaturisation or inflammation.

ul: Diffuse thinning; parted hair looks thinner; **no discrete bald patch**.
Increased daily shed; club hairs with a white bulb on the brush (photo teaching: D10).
Pull test: many club hairs come out easily when active.
Scalp skin looks normal; ostia preserved.
Pattern loss is gradual miniaturisation over years (male temples/vertex; female crown with widened part, frontal hairline usually kept).
Management (minoxidil, male finasteride MHRA mood warnings, etc.) is covered on the [androgenetic alopecia](condition:androgenetic-alopecia) page, with its own photo gallery.

ddx.name: Diffuse AA
ddx.f: Exclamation hairs, yellow dots, rapid patches

ul: Reassure: acute TE usually regrows over **6–12 months** once the trigger has passed; shedding can look alarming but follicles are alive.
Correct reversible causes (iron if deficient, thyroid replacement optimisation, review culprit drugs with the original prescriber).
Gentle hair care; avoid crash diets; camouflage if wanted.
Do not promise “hair vitamins” as evidence-based cure-alls.
If patterned miniaturisation coexists, manage as on the AGA page.
Refer if diagnostic doubt, progressive patterned loss with virilisation, scarring signs, or severe distress.

refer.t: Virilisation or sudden severe FPHL → endocrine/tumour pathways.
Patchy, scaly or shiny bald areas — not TE.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Virilisation or sudden severe FPHL → endocrine/tumour pathways.
Patchy, scaly or shiny bald areas — not TE.
Kerion — urgent antifungal pathway.
Anxiety; may unmask underlying androgenetic alopecia.
Acute TE resolves in most within 6–12 months; chronic TE fluctuates over years but rarely causes baldness.

pearls: Postpartum shedding is physiological — counsel antenatally when possible.
Teaching grid: TE (D09) vs FPHL (D06) vs extensive AA — different time courses and trichoscopy.

quiz.q: When should you think of Telogen effluvium?
quiz.a: Sudden increase in hairs in the brush or shower, diffuse thinning, no bald patches — often 2–3 months after illness, childbirth or a new drug.
A stressor synchronises many anagen follicles into telogen; club hairs shed together weeks later.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Identify the trigger, check thyroid/ferritin when indicated, reassure that acute TE usually settles in 6–12 months; treat coexistent pattern loss separately.
Patchy loss, scale, or lost ostia are not TE — rethink AA, tinea or scarring alopecia.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Virilisation or sudden severe FPHL → endocrine/tumour pathways.
